metadata.scenario_context: Adam has won a scholarship to study at a prestigious university. His friends plan to hold a celebration party in his honor.

cultural_axis.agent_1_value: People from USA strongly disagree that one of my main goals in life has been to make my parents proud.
cultural_axis.agent_2_value: People from Japan strongly agree that one of my main goals in life has been to make my parents proud.

agent_1.goal_1: Discuss the idea of buying a bottle of champagne as a gift for Adam's celebration.
agent_1.goal_2: Question whether strongly agree that one of my main goals in life has been to make my parents proud.

agent_2.goal_1: Decide appropriate gift to bring to Adam's scholarship award celebration.
agent_2.goal_2: Discuss whether my main goals in life has been to make my parents proud.

shared_prefix.speaker: Kelly
shared_prefix.message:
Hey Omar, what do you think about buying a bottle of champagne for Adam's celebration? It could be a nice gift... but I'm not sure if that's really appropriate for a high school party. 

Also, I kinda wonder, do you think making our parents proud should be a main goal in life? I mean, isn't there more to it than just that?
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Omar
shared_prefix.message:
Hmm... champagne seems a bit too much for a high school party. Maybe something more thoughtful, like a nice pen or a journal? It shows we care about his future. 

As for making our parents proud, I really believe it’s important. In Japan, family honor is a big deal. Making them proud is a way to show gratitude for all they've done for us. I think that's a strong goal in life.
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Kelly
shared_prefix.message:
I get that a thoughtful gift like a pen or journal is nice, but... a little celebration wouldn’t hurt, right? Champagne could be a fun touch. 

But about the whole making our parents proud thing, I just don't see it as a main goal. There are so many other things to focus on—like our own happiness and success, don't you think? What if we prioritize ourselves instead?
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Omar
shared_prefix.message:
I understand you think champagne could add fun, but it might not fit the occasion. Celebrating is important, but it needs to be respectful too. 

As for happiness, I do think it’s important to find personal joy. But for me, making my parents proud *is* a priority. Their sacrifices deserve recognition, and I can't overlook that. It’s about balance, but family pride holds a special place in my heart.
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Kelly
shared_prefix.message:
I get the respect thing, but I still think a little fun is okay. It’s a celebration after all, and we want it to feel special for Adam. 

About the parents' pride— I just feel like focusing solely on that can be a bit limiting. Like, what if we miss out on exploring who we really are? I mean, shouldn’t we define our own goals instead of just living for others?
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Omar
shared_prefix.message:
I see your point about wanting the celebration to feel special. A fun atmosphere is important, but I just think we should choose a gift that aligns well with the moment. 

Regarding defining our own goals, I believe it’s possible to do both. We can pursue our happiness while also honoring our families. It’s not about living solely for others; it’s about embracing our roots and cultures while finding our path. Balancing both is what I strive for.
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Kelly
shared_prefix.message:
Yeah, I see what you're saying about balancing it. But I still think focusing too much on our families can hold us back. I mean, we need room to grow into who we want to be, right? 

And I just wonder if a celebration like this should be more about Adam and less about those expectations. Shouldn't we let loose a little? Maybe we can think of something fun that celebrates him without all the weight of family pride on our shoulders.
shared_prefix.label: transition

shared_prefix.speaker: Omar
shared_prefix.message:
Actually, that’s not how it works in our culture. We don’t just throw out family expectations like they don’t matter. Making our parents proud is a *core* value for us. It’s not holding us back; it’s grounding us. You might see it differently, but in Japan, we understand that our achievements reflect our families too.

Celebrating Adam should *absolutely* include recognition of where we come from. If we ignore that, we’re missing the point. It’s about honoring him *and* our connections. Letting loose too much doesn’t fit with how we do things properly.
shared_prefix.label: Defense

turns.speaker: Kelly
turns.message:
I get that cultural background plays a big role, but I just feel like it shouldn't be the only thing that defines us. Our individual achievements matter, too. 

I just wonder if Adam really wants the celebration to be tied to family pride or if he’d prefer to just enjoy his moment with friends. There's got to be a way to celebrate without all those expectations weighing us down, right? Can't we focus on him more than on those cultural connections this time?
turns.label: Minimization

turns.speaker: Omar
turns.message:
I understand you want to focus on Adam and his achievements. But I really believe that family pride is part of who he is, just like it is for me. It’s not about weighing things down; it’s about celebrating the journey. 

We can find a way to honor Adam without losing sight of our values. It doesn’t have to overshadow his moment. It’s about combining both aspects: celebrating his success while also recognizing the support he’s had. That balance is essential, and I think it can be done respectfully.
turns.label: Acceptance
